claim: Axolotls are uniquely able to mobilize neural stem cells to regenerate all missing regions of the spinal cord.
source: Axolotls are uniquely able to mobilize neural stem cells to regenerate all missing regions of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including lineage tracing and regeneration experiments.

claim: During regeneration, axolotl neural stem cells repress neurogenic genes.
source: Here, we show that during regeneration, axolotl neural stem cells repress neurogenic genes and reactivate a transcriptional program similar to embryonic neuroepithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by NanoString gene expression data showing downregulation of neurogenic genes like Pax6, Pax7, and others during regeneration (Figure 1B, 1C, 1D).

claim: During regeneration, axolotl neural stem cells reactivate a transcriptional program similar to embryonic neuroepithelial cells.
source: Here, we show that during regeneration, axolotl neural stem cells repress neurogenic genes and reactivate a transcriptional program similar to embryonic neuroepithelial cells.
evidence: Supported by comparison of gene expression profiles between regenerating axolotl spinal cord and chick embryonic neuroepithelial cells (Figure 1B, 1C).

claim: Dedifferentiation during regeneration includes the acquisition of rapid cell cycles.
source: This dedifferentiation includes the acquisition of rapid cell cycles, the switch from neurogenic to proliferative divisions, and the re-expression of planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway components.
evidence: Supported by BrdU labeling experiments showing cell cycle length of 119 ± 10 hours in regenerating cells versus 324 ± 21 hours in uninjured cells (Figure 2F, 2G).

claim: Dedifferentiation during regeneration includes the switch from neurogenic to proliferative divisions.
source: This dedifferentiation includes the acquisition of rapid cell cycles, the switch from neurogenic to proliferative divisions, and the re-expression of planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway components.
evidence: Supported by EdU labeling showing 99% ± 1% of EdU+ cells remain SOX2+ in regenerating spinal cord versus 84% ± 2% in non-regenerating regions (Figure 2H).

claim: Dedifferentiation during regeneration includes the re-expression of planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway components.
source: This dedifferentiation includes the acquisition of rapid cell cycles, the switch from neurogenic to proliferative divisions, and the re-expression of planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway components.
evidence: Supported by NanoString data and in situ hybridization showing upregulation of Wnt5a, Wnt5b, and Prickle1 during regeneration (Figure 1B, 1E, Figure 3A, 3B).

claim: PCP induction is essential to reorient mitotic spindles along the anterior-posterior axis of elongation.
source: We show that PCP induction is essential to reorient mitotic spindles along the anterior-posterior axis of elongation, and orthogonal to the cell apical-basal axis.
evidence: Supported by analysis of mitotic spindle orientation showing cells within the Prickle1 zone divide parallel to the AP axis, and Prickle1 overexpression disrupts this orientation (Figure 4D, Figure 5C, 5D).

claim: Disruption of PCP-mediated spindle orientation results in premature neurogenesis.
source: Disruption of this property results in premature neurogenesis and halts regeneration.
evidence: Supported by EdU/Tuj1 labeling showing Vangl2 overexpression leads to 0.07 ± 0.01 fraction of EdU+ cells differentiating into neurons in regenerating spinal cord versus 0.01 ± 0.01 in controls (Figure 8B, 8C).

claim: Disruption of PCP-mediated spindle orientation halts regeneration.
source: Disruption of this property results in premature neurogenesis and halts regeneration.
evidence: Supported by measurements showing Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords are shorter than controls at day 4 and day 6 (Figure 6B).

claim: Cells with stem cell features persist throughout life lining the spinal cord central canal of the axolotl.
source: Cells with stem cell features persist throughout life lining the spinal cord central canal of the axolotl.
evidence: This is a statement in the Introduction supported by citation to previous work (Holder et al., 1991).

claim: Neural stem cells in the uninjured axolotl spinal cord divide occasionally to add neurons by asymmetric divisions.
source: These cells divide occasionally to add neurons to the intact central nervous system of the axolotl, presumably by asymmetric divisions (Holder et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Holder et al., 1991.

claim: Following tail amputation, the pool of SOX2+ neural stem cells located within 500 μm of the injury is mobilized to regenerate the missing portion of the spinal cord.
source: Following tail amputation, however, the pool of SOX2+ neural stem cells located within 500 μm of the injury is mobilized to regenerate the missing portion of the spinal cord (Fei et al., 2014; McHedlishvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fei et al., 2014 and McHedlishvili et al., 2007.

claim: SOX2+ cells proliferate extensively after tail amputation, expanding as a tube along the anterior-posterior axis.
source: First, these SOX2+ cells proliferate extensively, expanding as a tube along the anterior-posterior (AP) axis in concert with overall tail regeneration (Egar and Singer, 1972; Holtzer, 1956; McHedlishvili et al., 2007; Nordlander and Singer, 1978).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and by data in the manuscript showing exponential-like growth (Figure 2A).

claim: A few neurons from the source zone move and integrate into the regenerating cord, but their contribution is minimal as they do not dedifferentiate or divide.
source: Although a few neurons from the source zone move and integrate into the regenerating cord, their contribution is minimal as they do not seem to dedifferentiate or divide during the process (Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2003.

claim: SOX2+ cells closest to the amputation plane resume neurogenesis later during regeneration.
source: It is later on, when the SOX2+ cells closest to the amputation plane resume neurogenesis that the differentiated cell types of the new spinal cord are gradually replenished in a head-to-tail sequence while cells at the posterior end continue rapid expansion (Holtzer, 1956; McHedlishvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Holtzer, 1956 and McHedlishvili et al., 2007.

claim: Differentiated cell types of the new spinal cord are gradually replenished in a head-to-tail sequence.
source: It is later on, when the SOX2+ cells closest to the amputation plane resume neurogenesis that the differentiated cell types of the new spinal cord are gradually replenished in a head-to-tail sequence while cells at the posterior end continue rapid expansion (Holtzer, 1956; McHedlishvili et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Holtzer, 1956 and McHedlishvili et al., 2007.

claim: Lineage tracing showed that at least some cells in the source zone become highly proliferative and multipotent, populating different dorsal-ventral regions of the spinal cord.
source: Importantly, lineage tracing of cells lining the central canal showed that at least some cells in the source zone become highly proliferative and multipotent, populating different dorsal-ventral regions of the spinal cord (McHedlishvili et al., 2007; McHedlishvili et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McHedlishvili et al., 2007 and McHedlishvili et al., 2012.

claim: Clonal isolates, when transplanted into the regenerating spinal cord, contributed to neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes in all regions of the spinal cord.
source: Furthermore, clonal isolates, when transplanted into the regenerating spinal cord, contributed to neurons, astrocytes, as well as oligodendrocytes in all regions of the spinal cord, indicating that a single cell can give rise to all cells of the spinal cord (McHedlishvili et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to McHedlishvili et al., 2012.

claim: A single cell can give rise to all cells of the spinal cord.
source: Furthermore, clonal isolates, when transplanted into the regenerating spinal cord, contributed to neurons, astrocytes, as well as oligodendrocytes in all regions of the spinal cord, indicating that a single cell can give rise to all cells of the spinal cord (McHedlishvili et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the clonal transplantation experiments cited from McHedlishvili et al., 2012.

claim: Cells in the axolotl spinal cord display features of true stem cells, since they can self renew and give rise to all the differentiated cell types of the new spinal cord.
source: Thus, cells in the axolotl spinal cord display features of true stem cells, since they can self renew and give rise to all the differentiated cell types of the new spinal cord (Echeverri and Tanaka, 2002; McHedlishvili et al., 2007; McHedlishvili et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple cited studies (Echeverri and Tanaka, 2002; McHedlishvili et al., 2007; McHedlishvili et al., 2012).

claim: During spinal cord development, SOX2+ cells in the stem zone progressively coalesce to form the neural plate that then closes into the neural tube.
source: During spinal cord development, SOX2+ cells residing in the so-called stem zone (SZ) progressively coalesce to form the neural plate (pre-neural tube, PNT) that then closes into the neural tube (Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2009.

claim: PNT cells express Sox2 but do not yet express neuronal transcription factors and thus remain multipotent and proliferating.
source: Although PNT cells express Sox2 they do not yet express neuronal transcription factors and thus, remain multipotent and proliferating (del Corral et al., 2003; del Corral and Storey, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to del Corral et al., 2003 and del Corral and Storey, 2004.

claim: Cells in the neural tube acquire neural progenitor identity as they start expressing neuronal transcription factors and commit to produce the cell types of the adult spinal cord.
source: Cells in the neural tube acquire neural progenitor identity as they start expressing neuronal transcription factors and commit to produce the cell types of the adult spinal cord (del Corral et al., 2003; Jessell, 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to del Corral et al., 2003 and Jessell, 2000.

claim: 37 out of 50 chick genes low in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are downregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples compared to day 0.
source: Direct comparison of changes in gene expression between datasets showed that 37 out of 50 chick genes low in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are downregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples compared to day 0, and 18 out of 50 chick genes high in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are upregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples (significant association, p=0.001294 as result of Fisher's exact test on count data) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the NanoString gene expression analysis comparing axolotl regeneration to chick development data.

claim: 18 out of 50 chick genes high in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are upregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples.
source: Direct comparison of changes in gene expression between datasets showed that 37 out of 50 chick genes low in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are downregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples compared to day 0, and 18 out of 50 chick genes high in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are upregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples (significant association, p=0.001294 as result of Fisher's exact test on count data) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the NanoString gene expression analysis comparing axolotl regeneration to chick development data.

claim: The association between gene expression changes in axolotl regeneration and chick development is statistically significant (p=0.001294).
source: Direct comparison of changes in gene expression between datasets showed that 37 out of 50 chick genes low in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are downregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples compared to day 0, and 18 out of 50 chick genes high in the SZ+PNT versus CNT+RNT are upregulated in day 1 or day 6 axolotl samples (significant association, p=0.001294 as result of Fisher's exact test on count data) (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Fisher's exact test on the gene expression comparison data.

claim: Egr1 is highly upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Highly upregulated genes common to the SZ+PNT and the regenerating samples included the early growth response gene Egr1 (Milbrandt, 1987) and the estrogen-induced Greb1 (Ghosh et al., 2000), both associated with growth regulation (Liao et al., 2004; Rae et al., 2005); and the caudal gene Cdx4, a key player in embryonic body axis elongation (Faas and Isaacs, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2005; van Nes et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B) and in situ hybridization (Figure 1E).

claim: Greb1 is highly upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Highly upregulated genes common to the SZ+PNT and the regenerating samples included the early growth response gene Egr1 (Milbrandt, 1987) and the estrogen-induced Greb1 (Ghosh et al., 2000), both associated with growth regulation (Liao et al., 2004; Rae et al., 2005); and the caudal gene Cdx4, a key player in embryonic body axis elongation (Faas and Isaacs, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2005; van Nes et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B) and in situ hybridization (Figure 1E).

claim: Cdx4 is highly upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Highly upregulated genes common to the SZ+PNT and the regenerating samples included the early growth response gene Egr1 (Milbrandt, 1987) and the estrogen-induced Greb1 (Ghosh et al., 2000), both associated with growth regulation (Liao et al., 2004; Rae et al., 2005); and the caudal gene Cdx4, a key player in embryonic body axis elongation (Faas and Isaacs, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2005; van Nes et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B) and in situ hybridization (Figure 1E).

claim: Egr1 and Greb1 are associated with growth regulation.
source: Highly upregulated genes common to the SZ+PNT and the regenerating samples included the early growth response gene Egr1 (Milbrandt, 1987) and the estrogen-induced Greb1 (Ghosh et al., 2000), both associated with growth regulation (Liao et al., 2004; Rae et al., 2005); and the caudal gene Cdx4, a key player in embryonic body axis elongation (Faas and Isaacs, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2005; van Nes et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Liao et al., 2004 and Rae et al., 2005.

claim: Cdx4 is a key player in embryonic body axis elongation.
source: Highly upregulated genes common to the SZ+PNT and the regenerating samples included the early growth response gene Egr1 (Milbrandt, 1987) and the estrogen-induced Greb1 (Ghosh et al., 2000), both associated with growth regulation (Liao et al., 2004; Rae et al., 2005); and the caudal gene Cdx4, a key player in embryonic body axis elongation (Faas and Isaacs, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2005; van Nes et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Faas and Isaacs, 2009; Shimizu et al., 2005; and van Nes et al., 2006.

claim: Neuronal transcription factors Pax6, Pax7, Tfap2b, Prdm12, Irx1, Nr2f2, Dbx2, Zic1 and Hes6 are downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Conversely, a number of neuronal transcription factors that were higher in the neurogenic CNT+RNT than the SZ+PNT zone were downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord (Pax6, Pax7, Tfap2b, Prdm12 Irx1, Nr2f2, Dbx2, Zic1 and Hes6), along with genes related to signaling pathways that during embryonic development promote neurogenesis such as the retinoic acid signaling-readout genes Crabp1 and Rarb (del Corral et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B, 1C) and in situ hybridization for Pax6 and Pax7 (Figure 1D).

claim: Retinoic acid signaling-readout genes Crabp1 and Rarb are downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Conversely, a number of neuronal transcription factors that were higher in the neurogenic CNT+RNT than the SZ+PNT zone were downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord (Pax6, Pax7, Tfap2b, Prdm12 Irx1, Nr2f2, Dbx2, Zic1 and Hes6), along with genes related to signaling pathways that during embryonic development promote neurogenesis such as the retinoic acid signaling-readout genes Crabp1 and Rarb (del Corral et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B, 1C) and citation to del Corral et al., 2003.

claim: Retinoic acid signaling promotes neurogenesis during embryonic development.
source: Conversely, a number of neuronal transcription factors that were higher in the neurogenic CNT+RNT than the SZ+PNT zone were downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord (Pax6, Pax7, Tfap2b, Prdm12 Irx1, Nr2f2, Dbx2, Zic1 and Hes6), along with genes related to signaling pathways that during embryonic development promote neurogenesis such as the retinoic acid signaling-readout genes Crabp1 and Rarb (del Corral et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to del Corral et al., 2003.

claim: Bmpr1b is downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor Bmpr1b and the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor Fgfr2, both linked to neurogenic differentiation during development and as such more highly expressed in the CNT+RNT than in the SZ+PNT (Panchision et al., 2001, Zhang et al., 2002), were downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1C) and citations to Panchision et al., 2001 and Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: Fgfr2 is downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor Bmpr1b and the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor Fgfr2, both linked to neurogenic differentiation during development and as such more highly expressed in the CNT+RNT than in the SZ+PNT (Panchision et al., 2001, Zhang et al., 2002), were downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1C) and citations to Panchision et al., 2001 and Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: Bmpr1b and Fgfr2 are linked to neurogenic differentiation during development.
source: Intriguingly, the expression of the bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) receptor Bmpr1b and the fibroblast growth factor (FGF) receptor Fgfr2, both linked to neurogenic differentiation during development and as such more highly expressed in the CNT+RNT than in the SZ+PNT (Panchision et al., 2001, Zhang et al., 2002), were downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Panchision et al., 2001 and Zhang et al., 2002.

claim: EphA1 receptor is upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Likewise, the expression patterns of Eph receptors in the proliferative SZ+PNT seem to be recapitulated in the regenerating spinal cord with the upregulation of EphA1 receptor and continued, although lower, expression of EphA5 in comparison with the uninjured spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1C).

claim: EphA5 shows continued, although lower, expression in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
source: Likewise, the expression patterns of Eph receptors in the proliferative SZ+PNT seem to be recapitulated in the regenerating spinal cord with the upregulation of EphA1 receptor and continued, although lower, expression of EphA5 in comparison with the uninjured spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1C).

claim: Eph family of receptor tyrosine kinases have been implicated in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation of neural progenitors, neuron survival, axon regrowth and axon sprouting.
source: The Eph family of receptor tyrosine kinases have been implicated among others in regulating cell proliferation and differentiation of neural progenitors, neuron survival, axon regrowth and axon sprouting, in the developing and adult nervous system (Conover et al., 2000; Khodosevich et al., 2011; North et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Conover et al., 2000; Khodosevich et al., 2011; and North et al., 2009.

claim: Eph receptor activities depend on the combination of Eph receptor and ephrins.
source: Their activities depend on the combination of Eph receptor and ephrins (Eph receptor interacting proteins) (Dodelet and Pasquale, 2000; Lisabeth et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Dodelet and Pasquale, 2000 and Lisabeth et al., 2013.

claim: MAPK signaling is presumably more active in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord.
source: In that line, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling is presumably more active in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord, based on the strong upregulation of its transcriptional target gene Rasgrp3 and downregulation of the negative regulator Dusp4.
evidence: This is an inference based on gene expression changes (upregulation of Rasgrp3 and downregulation of Dusp4) observed in NanoString data.

claim: Rasgrp3 is strongly upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: In that line, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling is presumably more active in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord, based on the strong upregulation of its transcriptional target gene Rasgrp3 and downregulation of the negative regulator Dusp4.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1C).

claim: Dusp4 is downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord.
source: In that line, mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling is presumably more active in the regenerating spinal cord compared to the uninjured spinal cord, based on the strong upregulation of its transcriptional target gene Rasgrp3 and downregulation of the negative regulator Dusp4.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1C).

claim: FGF2 has been shown to be upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord of another salamander species.
source: However, although other FGFs were not present in the 100-gene list, FGF2 has been shown to be upregulated in the regenerating spinal cord of in another salamander species and thus could be activating MAPK signaling in the context of spinal cord regeneration (Zhang et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2000.

claim: Non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling is activated during regeneration, reflected in the strong upregulation of Wnt5a, Wnt5b, and Prickle1 genes.
source: Although a more extensive analysis of signalling activities during axolotl spinal cord regeneration will require a global genome-wide approach, the activation of non-canonical Wnt/PCP signaling during regeneration, reflected in the strong upregulation of Wnt5a, Wnt5b, Prickle1 genes, was notable in our dataset.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B, 1C) and in situ hybridization (Figure 1E, Figure 3A, 3B).

claim: Wnt5a, Wnt5b, and Prickle1 genes are highly upregulated in the developmental SZ+PNT sample.
source: These genes are also highly upregulated in the developmental SZ+PNT sample, consistent with the notion that regenerating neural stem cells in the axolotl dedifferentiate to a SZ+PNT-like state.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by comparison with chick developmental data (Figure 1C).

claim: Sox2 transcript levels do not visibly change during regeneration.
source: To confirm that the gene expression changes occurred within the neural stem cells we performed in situ hybridization of selected factors. While transcript levels of the neural stem cell marker Sox2 did not visibly change during regeneration, the neuronal transcription factors Pax6 and Pax7 and the glial marker Gfap showed indeed lower expression levels in Sox2+ cells at day 1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1D).

claim: Pax6 and Pax7 show lower expression levels in Sox2+ cells at day 1.
source: To confirm that the gene expression changes occurred within the neural stem cells we performed in situ hybridization of selected factors. While transcript levels of the neural stem cell marker Sox2 did not visibly change during regeneration, the neuronal transcription factors Pax6 and Pax7 and the glial marker Gfap showed indeed lower expression levels in Sox2+ cells at day 1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1D).

claim: Gfap shows lower expression levels in Sox2+ cells at day 1.
source: To confirm that the gene expression changes occurred within the neural stem cells we performed in situ hybridization of selected factors. While transcript levels of the neural stem cell marker Sox2 did not visibly change during regeneration, the neuronal transcription factors Pax6 and Pax7 and the glial marker Gfap showed indeed lower expression levels in Sox2+ cells at day 1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1D).

claim: Egr1, Cdx4, Greb1, and Prickle1 show induction of signal in Sox2+ cells at day 1 or day 6.
source: Conversely, examination of upregulated genes such as Egr1 at day 1 and Cdx4, Greb1, and PCP gene Prickle1 at day 6 showed an induction of signal in Sox2+ cells of regenerating samples (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 1E).

claim: Embryonic PNT neuroepithelium has marked apical-basal polarity including the expression of tight junction proteins.
source: A distinctive characteristic of embryonic PNT neuroepithelium is its marked apical-basal polarity including the expression of tight junction proteins (Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996.

claim: Occludin and claudin-5 are expressed in PNT cells but downregulated at the onset of neurogenesis.
source: To extend the findings above, we immunostained axolotl spinal cord cross-sections for the tight junction proteins occludin (OCLN) and claudin-5 (CLDN5), previously shown to be expressed in PNT cells but downregulated at the onset of neurogenesis (Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Aaku-Saraste et al., 1996.

claim: Strong OCLN and CLDN5 signal is observed in the apical side of regenerating neural stem cells compared to cells in the uninjured spinal cord.
source: We observed strong OCLN and CLDN5 signal in the apical side of regenerating neural stem cells compared to cells in the uninjured spinal cord, while the junctional protein ZO-1 did not change (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1F).

claim: ZO-1 expression does not change between regenerating and uninjured neural stem cells.
source: We observed strong OCLN and CLDN5 signal in the apical side of regenerating neural stem cells compared to cells in the uninjured spinal cord, while the junctional protein ZO-1 did not change (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 1F).

claim: Embryonic neural progenitors lengthen their cell cycle as they switch from symmetric, proliferative divisions to asymmetric, neurogenic divisions.
source: A functional characteristic of embryonic neural progenitors is the lengthening of their cell cycle as they switch from symmetric, proliferative divisions to asymmetric, neurogenic divisions (Calegari et al., 2005; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 1995; Wilcock et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Calegari et al., 2005; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2014; Takahashi et al., 1995; and Wilcock et al., 2007.

claim: The spinal cord shows exponential-like growth during the first 8 days after amputation.
source: The exponential-like growth of the spinal cord during the first 8 days after amputation indeed seemed to support this idea (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by growth measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The difference in the fraction of PCNA+ cells is surprisingly small between the non-regenerating and regenerating spinal cord.
source: The difference in the fraction of PCNA+ cells was surprisingly small between the non-regenerating and regenerating spinal cord (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A low percentage of SOX2+PCNA+ cells in the uninjured spinal cord are mitotic.
source: Mitotic index quantifications (see Materials and methods), however, revealed that a low percentage of these SOX2+PCNA+ cells in the uninjured spinal cord are mitotic (Figure 2D, day 0).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mitotic index data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There is a stable, threefold increase in mitotic figures in the source zone and regenerating spinal cord by day 4.
source: In contrast, we found a stable, threefold increase in mitotic figures in the source zone and regenerating spinal cord by day 4 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by mitotic index data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Most cells in non-regenerative populations (0.80 ± 0.01 in uninjured and 0.82 ± 0.01 in non-regenerating region) take up BrdU.
source: In line with PCNA results, most cells in non-regenerative populations (0.80 ± 0.01 and 0.82 ± 0.01 in uninjured and non-regenerating region of the spinal cord, respectively) and almost all cells in the regenerating spinal cord took up BrdU (0.96 ± 0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by BrdU labeling data (Figure 2F).

claim: Almost all cells in the regenerating spinal cord (0.96 ± 0.01) take up BrdU.
source: In line with PCNA results, most cells in non-regenerative populations (0.80 ± 0.01 and 0.82 ± 0.01 in uninjured and non-regenerating region of the spinal cord, respectively) and almost all cells in the regenerating spinal cord took up BrdU (0.96 ± 0.01).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by BrdU labeling data (Figure 2F).

claim: The time needed to completely label the proliferating population of the regenerating spinal cord is ~31 hours.
source: However, the time needed to completely label the proliferating population of the regenerating spinal cord was much shorter (~31 h) than the time required for complete labeling of the uninjured (~192 h) and non-regenerating (~185 h) populations, suggesting that regenerating neural stem cells progress much faster through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by BrdU labeling data (Figure 2F).

claim: The time required for complete BrdU labeling of the uninjured population is ~192 hours.
source: However, the time needed to completely label the proliferating population of the regenerating spinal cord was much shorter (~31 h) than the time required for complete labeling of the uninjured (~192 h) and non-regenerating (~185 h) populations, suggesting that regenerating neural stem cells progress much faster through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by BrdU labeling data (Figure 2F).

claim: The time required for complete BrdU labeling of the non-regenerating population is ~185 hours.
source: However, the time needed to completely label the proliferating population of the regenerating spinal cord was much shorter (~31 h) than the time required for complete labeling of the uninjured (~192 h) and non-regenerating (~185 h) populations, suggesting that regenerating neural stem cells progress much faster through the cell cycle.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by BrdU labeling data (Figure 2F).

claim: Uninjured neural stem cells have an average cell cycle of 324 h ± 21 h.
source: These calculations indicated that uninjured and non-regenerating populations have an average cell cycle of 324 h ± 21 h and 339 h ± 32 h, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell cycle modeling from BrdU data (Figure 2G).

claim: Non-regenerating neural stem cells have an average cell cycle of 339 h ± 32 h.
source: These calculations indicated that uninjured and non-regenerating populations have an average cell cycle of 324 h ± 21 h and 339 h ± 32 h, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell cycle modeling from BrdU data (Figure 2G).

claim: Regenerating cells undergo significantly shorter cell cycles (119 h ± 10 h).
source: In contrast, regenerating cells undergo significantly shorter cell cycles (119 h ± 10 h).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell cycle modeling from BrdU data (Figure 2G).

claim: The difference in cell cycle length arises largely from a shorter G1 phase in regenerative cells compared to non-regenerative cells but also a shorter S phase.
source: These differences arise largely from a shorter G1 phase in regenerative cells compared to non-regenerative cells but also a shorter S phase.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell cycle phase calculations (Figure 2G).

claim: In the non-regenerating region, 84% ± 2% of the EdU+ cells are SOX2+.
source: While in the non-regenerating region 84% ± 2% of the EdU+ cells were SOX2+, in the regenerating spinal cord virtually all EdU+ cells were SOX2+ (99% ± 1%) (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU/SOX2 labeling data (Figure 2H).

claim: In the regenerating spinal cord, virtually all EdU+ cells are SOX2+ (99% ± 1%).
source: While in the non-regenerating region 84% ± 2% of the EdU+ cells were SOX2+, in the regenerating spinal cord virtually all EdU+ cells were SOX2+ (99% ± 1%) (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU/SOX2 labeling data (Figure 2H).

claim: Non-regenerating cells exit the cell cycle to produce SOX2- neurons, whereas regenerating cells undergo proliferative divisions at least during the first 8 days of regeneration.
source: These observations indicated that whereas non-regenerating cells presumably exit the cell cycle to produce SOX2- neurons, regenerating cells undergo proliferative divisions at least during the first 8 days of regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference from the EdU/SOX2 labeling data (Figure 2H).

claim: After a full cell cycle, only 70% of the EdU+ cells in the non-regenerating portion would express SOX2.
source: Normalizing for this difference, we would expect that after a full cell cycle, only 70% of the EdU+ cells in the non-regenerating portion would express SOX2.
evidence: This is a calculation based on normalizing for differences in cell cycle length between regenerating and non-regenerating populations.

claim: Neural stem cells speed up their cell cycle as they switch from a neurogenic to a proliferative mode of division that leads to the exponential-like growth of the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Together, these results indicate that neural stem cells speed up their cell cycle as they switch from a neurogenic to a proliferative mode of division that leads to the exponential-like growth of the regenerating spinal cord.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple pieces of data including cell cycle measurements and EdU labeling.

claim: Wnt5a, Wnt5b, and Prickle1 constituted three of the most upregulated genes in the regenerating spinal cord dataset.
source: Wnt5a, Wnt5b, and the core PCP gene Prickle1 (Gray et al., 2011) constituted three of the most upregulated genes in our regenerating spinal cord dataset (Figure 1B and Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by NanoString data (Figure 1B, Figure 3A).

claim: Prickle1 is a core PCP gene.
source: Wnt5a, Wnt5b, and the core PCP gene Prickle1 (Gray et al., 2011) constituted three of the most upregulated genes in our regenerating spinal cord dataset (Figure 1B and Figure 3A).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Gray et al., 2011.

claim: Wnts like Wnt5a can signal through the PCP pathway to drive tissue growth and morphogenesis during embryonic development.
source: Because Wnts, like Wnt5a, can signal through the PCP pathway to drive tissue growth and morphogenesis during embryonic development (Gao et al., 2011; Wallingford, 2012), we set out to investigate how this pathway may be contributing to the efficient, tube-like extension of the neural stem cell pool during regeneration.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2011 and Wallingford, 2012.

claim: Wnt5a and Wnt5b transcripts show graded upregulation precisely in the regeneration source zone 1 day after amputation.
source: Intriguingly, we found graded upregulation of Wnt5a and Wnt5b transcripts precisely in the regeneration source zone 1 day after amputation (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3B).

claim: Prickle1 upregulation follows from day 3 and continues to be expressed in the caudal-most region of the regenerating spinal cord.
source: The upregulation of Prickle1 followed from day 3 and continued to be expressed in the caudal-most region of the regenerating spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3C, 3D).

claim: The Prickle1 zone is 429 ± 32 μm at day 3.
source: As the regenerating spinal cord grew along its AP axis, the Prickle1 zone increased in size (429 ± 32 μm at day 3 and 981 ± 74 μm at day 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by measurements from in situ hybridization (Figure 3C).

claim: The Prickle1 zone is 981 ± 74 μm at day 6.
source: As the regenerating spinal cord grew along its AP axis, the Prickle1 zone increased in size (429 ± 32 μm at day 3 and 981 ± 74 μm at day 6).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by measurements from in situ hybridization (Figure 3C).

claim: At day 14, the Prickle1 zone covers the caudal-most ~1600 μm of the regenerating spinal cord (1579 ± 75 μm).
source: At day 14, the Prickle1 zone covered the caudal-most ~1600 μm of the regenerating spinal cord (1579 ± 75 μm) but Prickle1 transcripts returned to undetectable levels close to the amputation plane (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by measurements from in situ hybridization (Figure 3C, 3D).

claim: Prickle1 transcripts return to undetectable levels close to the amputation plane at day 14.
source: At day 14, the Prickle1 zone covered the caudal-most ~1600 μm of the regenerating spinal cord (1579 ± 75 μm) but Prickle1 transcripts returned to undetectable levels close to the amputation plane (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization data (Figure 3D).

claim: The Prickle1 zone correlates with regions of a simple neuroepithelial structure that have yet to initiate robust neurogenesis.
source: Remarkably, the Prickle1 zone correlated with regions of a simple neuroepithelial structure that have yet to initiate robust neurogenesis (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by in situ hybridization showing Prickle1 expression in simple neuroepithelium (Figure 3D).

claim: Oriented cell divisions are a classical read-out of PCP in proliferating and elongating tissues.
source: Because oriented cell divisions are a classical read-out of PCP in proliferating and elongating tissues (Fischer et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2004; Matsuyama et al., 2009; Quesada-Hernandez et al., 2010; Saburi et al., 2008), we set out to investigate the spatial aspects of cell division in the regenerating spinal cord.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2004; Matsuyama et al., 2009; Quesada-Hernandez et al., 2010; and Saburi et al., 2008.

claim: Cells within the Prickle1 zone are significantly biased to divide parallel to the AP axis.
source: We found that cells within the Prickle1 zone were significantly biased to divide parallel to the AP axis, whereas cells outside of the Prickle1 zone divided randomly (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis of mitotic spindle orientation (Figure 4D).

claim: Cells outside of the Prickle1 zone divide randomly.
source: We found that cells within the Prickle1 zone were significantly biased to divide parallel to the AP axis, whereas cells outside of the Prickle1 zone divided randomly (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis of mitotic spindle orientation (Figure 4D).

claim: PCP mechanisms involve the polarized localization of the core PCP machinery.
source: PCP mechanisms involve the polarized localization of the core PCP machinery.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge about PCP mechanisms.

claim: Overexpression of core PCP components overwhelms the localization machinery and disorients PCP.
source: The function of PCP in many tissues has been tested via overexpression of core PCP components which presumably overwhelms the localization machinery and therefore disorients PCP (reviewed in [Gray et al., 2011]) (Carreira-Barbosa et al., 2003; Cho et al., 2015; Goto and Keller, 2002; Gubb et al., 1999; Jessen et al., 2002; Tree et al., 2002; Wallingford and Harland, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations including a review by Gray et al., 2011 and several primary studies.

claim: Deletion or overexpression of Prickle randomizes cell polarization cell autonomously only in those cells in which Prickle expression levels are deranged.
source: Deletion or overexpression of certain core PCP components such as Prickle randomize cell polarization cell autonomously only in those cells in which Prickle expression levels are deranged (Adler et al., 2000; Gubb and Garcia-Bellido, 1982; Lawrence et al., 2004; Strutt and Strutt, 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Adler et al., 2000; Gubb and Garcia-Bellido, 1982; Lawrence et al., 2004; and Strutt and Strutt, 2007.

claim: Vangl2 yields non cell-autonomous defects in PCP both in the cells with expression defects as well as their surrounding neighbors.
source: In contrast, a second class, which includes Vangl2, yields non cell-autonomous defects in PCP both in the cells with expression defects as well as their surrounding neighbors (Vinson and Adler, 1987).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Vinson and Adler, 1987.

claim: The lack or excess of Vangl2 in vertebrates propagates polarity defects non-cell autonomously, spreading the PCP defect through the tissue.
source: Similarly, the lack or excess of Vangl2 in vertebrates propagates polarity defects non-cell autonomously, spreading the PCP defect through the tissue (Darken et al., 2002; Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Mitchell et al., 2009; Montcouquiol et al., 2006; Sienknecht et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Darken et al., 2002; Devenport and Fuchs, 2008; Mitchell et al., 2009; Montcouquiol et al., 2006; and Sienknecht et al., 2011.

claim: Prickle1 overexpression results in 10-fold higher Prickle1 expression at day 6 compared to controls.
source: Quantitative real time PCR confirmed 10-fold higher Prickle1 expression at day 6 in Prickle1-electroporated spinal cords than in controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by qRT-PCR data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: On average, 21.5% of the spinal cord cells overexpress Prickle1 after electroporation.
source: However, because on average only 21.5% of the spinal cord cells overexpressed Prickle1 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), the levels of Prickle1 per electroporated cell were actually much higher.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by quantification data (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).

claim: mCherry-only electroporated cells display the same bias to divide parallel to the AP axis within the Prickle1 zone as in non-electroporated animals.
source: Analysis of mCherry-only electroporated cells indicated that these cells displayed the same bias to divide parallel to the AP axis within the Prickle1 zone as in non-electroporated animals (Figure 5C and Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis of mitotic spindle orientation (Figure 5C, Figure 4D).

claim: The bias in division orientation is lost in Prickle1-overexpressing cells.
source: In contrast, this bias in division orientation was lost in Prickle1-overexpressing cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by analysis of mitotic spindle orientation (Figure 5D).

claim: Prickle1-overexpressing cells continue to divide at a similar rate as control-electroporated cells.
source: Prickle1-overexpressing cells, however, continued to divide at a similar rate than control-electroporated cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU labeling data (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).

claim: PCP operates during spinal cord regeneration and one of its roles is to orient the axis of cell division along the rapidly elongating AP axis.
source: Thus, PCP operates during spinal cord regeneration and one of its roles is to orient the axis of cell division along the rapidly elongating AP axis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Prickle1 overexpression experiments showing loss of oriented divisions.

claim: Spinal cords overexpressing Vangl2 are shorter than controls at day 4 and day 6.
source: Measurements of spinal cord outgrowth at day 4 and day 6 showed that spinal cords overexpressing Vangl2 were shorter than controls (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by spinal cord length measurements (Figure 6B).

claim: A greater number of SOX2+ cells are counted on cross-sections of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords compared to controls.
source: Indeed, we counted a greater number of SOX2+ cells on cross-sections of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords compared to controls (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cell counting data (Figure 6C).

claim: PCP mechanisms are required for efficient extension of the regenerating spinal cord.
source: Together, these observations point to the classical shorter and broader PCP phenotype and confirm that PCP mechanisms are required for efficient extension of the regenerating spinal cord.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Vangl2 overexpression experiments showing shorter, broader spinal cords.

claim: During development, vertical cleavage planes with respect to the apical surface of the neural tube result in symmetric proliferative divisions, leading to the expansion of the early neuroepithelial cell pool.
source: During development, such vertical cleavage planes with respect to the apical surface of the neural tube result in symmetric proliferative divisions, leading to the expansion of the early neuroepithelial cell pool (Chenn and McConnell, 1995; Das and Storey, 2012; Peyre and Morin, 2012; Xie et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Chenn and McConnell, 1995; Das and Storey, 2012; Peyre and Morin, 2012; and Xie et al., 2013.

claim: Control-electroporated spinal cords show a tight distribution of vertically oriented cleavage planes.
source: We found a tight distribution of vertically oriented cleavage planes in control-electroporated spinal cords, whereas mitotic cells within the regenerating stem cell pool of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords displayed a more variable distribution of cleavage planes (Figure 7C), indicating a relaxation in the constraint to divide with vertical cleavage planes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cleavage plane angle measurements (Figure 7C).

claim: Mitotic cells within the regenerating stem cell pool of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords display a more variable distribution of cleavage planes.
source: We found a tight distribution of vertically oriented cleavage planes in control-electroporated spinal cords, whereas mitotic cells within the regenerating stem cell pool of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords displayed a more variable distribution of cleavage planes (Figure 7C), indicating a relaxation in the constraint to divide with vertical cleavage planes.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by cleavage plane angle measurements (Figure 7C).

claim: At day 4, the density of PH3+ cells is similar in control and Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords.
source: Interestingly, at day 4 the density of PH3+ cells was similar in control and Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PH3+ cell quantification (Figure 7D).

claim: By day 6, the density of PH3+ cells is significantly reduced in the regenerative regions of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords compared to controls.
source: By day 6, however, the density of PH3+ cells was significantly reduced in the regenerative regions of Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords compared to controls, that must undergo symmetric proliferative divisions.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by PH3+ cell quantification (Figure 7D).

claim: The reduction in PH3+ cells is not due to increased apoptosis.
source: This reduction was not due to increased apoptosis as we did not observe a significant difference in the number of caspase-3+ cells between control and Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords up to this time point (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by caspase-3 quantification (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Disruption of PCP did not affect the onset of rapid proliferative divisions.
source: These data suggested that disruption of PCP did not affect the onset of rapid proliferative divisions, since in both samples, we observed the initial increase in mitotic figures at day 4 after amputation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that PH3+ cell density is similar at day 4 in control and Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords.

claim: A substantial number of EdU+ cells differentiate into neurons within the 6-day labeling period in the non-regenerating region of the spinal cord.
source: In agreement with BrdU experiments (Figure 2H), a substantial number of EdU+ cells differentiated into neurons within the 6-day labeling period in the non-regenerating region of the spinal cord, and Vangl2 overexpression had no effect on the fraction of neurons formed (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU/Tuj1 labeling data (Figure 8B).

claim: Vangl2 overexpression has no effect on the fraction of neurons formed in the non-regenerating region.
source: In agreement with BrdU experiments (Figure 2H), a substantial number of EdU+ cells differentiated into neurons within the 6-day labeling period in the non-regenerating region of the spinal cord, and Vangl2 overexpression had no effect on the fraction of neurons formed (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU/Tuj1 labeling data (Figure 8B).

claim: Practically no neurons are born during the labeling time in the regenerating region of control spinal cords.
source: However, while practically no neurons were born during the labeling time in the regenerating region of control spinal cords, we found a significant number of newborn neurons in Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU/Tuj1 labeling data (Figure 8B, 8C).

claim: A significant number of newborn neurons are found in Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords during the labeling time.
source: However, while practically no neurons were born during the labeling time in the regenerating region of control spinal cords, we found a significant number of newborn neurons in Vangl2-overexpressing spinal cords (Figure 8B,C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by EdU/Tuj1 labeling data (Figure 8B, 8C).

claim: PCP is an essential mediator of the switch from neurogenic divisions to proliferative divisions during the first 8 days of regeneration.
source: Taken together, these findings indicate that PCP is an essential mediator of the switch from the neurogenic divisions seen in the uninjured spinal cord to the proliferative divisions observed in the regenerating spinal cord at least during the first 8 days of regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Vangl2 overexpression experiments showing premature neurogenesis.

claim: Perturbing PCP by overexpression of Vangl2 results in more variable mitotic cleavage planes and premature neurogenesis that reduces the numbers of proliferative cells and hampers regenerative spinal cord growth.
source: Perturbing PCP by overexpression of Vangl2 results in more variable mitotic cleavage planes and premature neurogenesis that presumably reduces the numbers of proliferative cells and hampers regenerative spinal cord growth.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple pieces of data from Vangl2 overexpression experiments.

claim: In mammals, spinal cord lesions induce neural stem cells to proliferate and give rise mainly to scar-forming astrocytes and oligodendrocytes.
source: In mammals, spinal cord lesions induce neural stem cells to proliferate and give rise mainly to scar-forming astrocytes and oligodendrocytes (Barnabe-Heider et al., 2010; Meletis et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Barnabe-Heider et al., 2010 and Meletis et al., 2008.

claim: The glial scar tissue is important for maintaining the integrity of the injured spinal cord.
source: The resulting glial scar tissue, although important for maintaining the integrity of the injured spinal cord (Sabelstrom et al., 2013), inhibits axon regrowth limiting functional recovery (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014; Frisen et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sabelstrom et al., 2013.

claim: Glial scar tissue inhibits axon regrowth limiting functional recovery.
source: The resulting glial scar tissue, although important for maintaining the integrity of the injured spinal cord (Sabelstrom et al., 2013), inhibits axon regrowth limiting functional recovery (Burda and Sofroniew, 2014; Frisen et al., 1995).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Burda and Sofroniew, 2014 and Frisen et al., 1995.

claim: In zebrafish, neural stem cells react to spinal cord lesions by increasing their local neurogenic output.
source: In zebrafish, neural stem cells react to spinal cord lesions by increasing their local neurogenic output (Kuscha et al., 2012; Reimer et al., 2013; Reimer et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Kuscha et al., 2012; Reimer et al., 2013; and Reimer et al., 2008.

claim: In zebrafish, a thin glial 'bridge' restores tissue integrity and function after spinal cord lesion.
source: Although a thin glial 'bridge' restores tissue integrity and function (Goldshmit et al., 2012), the spinal cord tissue architecture is not restored after lesion.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Goldshmit et al., 2012.

claim: In zebrafish, the spinal cord tissue architecture is not restored after lesion.
source: Although a thin glial 'bridge' restores tissue integrity and function (Goldshmit et al., 2012), the spinal cord tissue architecture is not restored after lesion.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Goldshmit et al., 2012.

claim: Complete restoration of missing regions of the axolotl spinal cord involves the re-expression of developmental cassettes associated with embryonic neuroepithelial cells of the PNT.
source: Here, we find that complete restoration of missing regions of the axolotl spinal cord involves the re-expression of developmental cassettes associated with embryonic neuroepithelial cells of the PNT (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a summary statement supported by the gene expression analysis comparing regeneration to development (Figure 1).

claim: The striking correspondence between downregulated genes at the onset of regeneration with those that were low in the embryonic SZ+PNT suggests that regenerating neural stem cells lose pro-neurogenic features and acquire a more multipotent phenotype.
source: The striking correspondence between downregulated genes at the onset of regeneration with those that were low in the embryonic SZ+PNT (Olivera-Martinez et al., 2014) suggests that regenerating neural stem cells lose pro-neurogenic features and acquire a more multipotent phenotype.
evidence: This is an inference from the gene expression comparison data (Figure 1C) and citation to Olivera-Martinez et al., 2014.

claim: Clonal tracing studies and implanted clonally-derived neurospheres previously pointed out that multipotent neural stem cells exist during regeneration in the axolotl.
source: Indeed, clonal tracing studies (McHedlishvili et al., 2007) and the fact that implanted clonally-derived neurospheres can reconstitute a complete spinal cord after tail amputation previously pointed out that multipotent neural stem cells exist during regeneration in the axolotl (McHedlishvili et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to McHedlishvili et al., 2007 and McHedlishvili et al., 2012.

claim: The redeployment or fine-tuning of signals that played a role during embryonic development are required for spinal cord regeneration in the axolotl.
source: Although regeneration-specific factors may exist, our study shows that the redeployment or fine-tuning of signals that played a role during embryonic development are required for spinal cord regeneration in the axolotl.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that developmental gene expression programs are reactivated during regeneration.

claim: During development, the onset of retinoic acid signalling halts the expansion of neural progenitors and drives them to make neurons in the developing spinal cord.
source: For example, during development the onset of retinoic acid signalling halts the expansion of neural progenitors and drives them to make neurons in the developing spinal cord.
evidence: This is a statement of established developmental biology knowledge.

claim: Retinoic acid-target genes become downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord, suggesting that signals that promote neurogenesis programs are shut down to allow the execution of self-renewing, multipotent programs during regeneration.
source: In our gene expression analysis, retinoic acid-target genes such as Rarb, Crabp1, and Meis2, become downregulated in the regenerating spinal cord, suggesting that signals that promote neurogenesis programs are shut down to possibly allow the execution of self-renewing, multipotent programs during regeneration.
evidence: This is an inference from the gene expression data showing downregulation of retinoic acid target genes.

claim: During regeneration, the implementation of PCP mechanisms coordinately orients tubular outgrowth and switches the mode of cell division from a neurogenic to an expansive, proliferative mode of division.
source: An important aspect of our findings is that, during regeneration, the implementation of PCP mechanisms coordinately orients tubular outgrowth and switches the mode of cell division from a neurogenic to an expansive, proliferative mode of division.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings about PCP function during regeneration.

claim: PCP has previously been implicated in the extension of tubular structures such as kidney tubules.
source: PCP has previously been implicated in the extension of tubular structures such as kidney tubules (Fischer et al., 2006; Karner et al., 2009; Lienkamp et al., 2012) and on the other hand has been associated with expansion of muscle satellite stem cells (Le Grand et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Fischer et al., 2006; Karner et al., 2009; and Lienkamp et al., 2012.

claim: PCP has been associated with expansion of muscle satellite stem cells.
source: PCP has previously been implicated in the extension of tubular structures such as kidney tubules (Fischer et al., 2006; Karner et al., 2009; Lienkamp et al., 2012) and on the other hand has been associated with expansion of muscle satellite stem cells (Le Grand et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Le Grand et al., 2009.

claim: In the developing mouse brain, Vangl2 malfunction interferes with normal spindle positioning and leads to premature terminal differentiation of neural progenitors.
source: In the developing mouse brain, Vangl2 malfunction interferes with normal spindle positioning and leads to premature terminal differentiation of neural progenitors (Lake and Sokol, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Lake and Sokol, 2009.

claim: In the regenerating axolotl spinal cord, both aspects of PCP (orientation and proliferation) appear to operate simultaneously to elicit efficient expansion of the neural stem cell pool in a tubular form.
source: In the regenerating axolotl spinal cord both aspects of PCP appear to operate simultaneously to elicit efficient expansion of the neural stem cell pool in a tubular form.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings showing PCP controls both division orientation and proliferative mode.

claim: The extension of the regenerating spinal cord tube may also rely on other proliferation-independent, PCP-oriented cell behaviors such as convergence and extension.
source: Although here we have focused on the role of PCP in controlling the orientation of cell division, the extension of the regenerating spinal cord tube may also rely on other proliferation-independent, PCP-oriented cell behaviors such as convergence and extension (Wallingford, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation about additional PCP mechanisms that may contribute to spinal cord extension, supported by citation to Wallingford, 2012.

claim: In the vertebrate embryo, Wnt5a gradients often establish PCP to orient cell behaviors driving the elongation of multiple developing tissues.
source: In the vertebrate embryo, Wnt5a gradients often establish PCP to orient cell behaviors driving the elongation of multiple developing tissues (Gao et al., 2011; Yamaguchi et al., 1999).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Gao et al., 2011 and Yamaguchi et al., 1999.

claim: Graded Wnt5a and Wnt5b upregulation is a common feature of regenerative systems such as the lizard tail, the salamander limb, and the tail and spinal cord of salamander, fish, and Xenopus.
source: Intriguingly, graded Wnt5a and Wnt5b upregulation is a common feature of regenerative systems such as the lizard tail (Hutchins et al., 2014), the salamander limb (Ghosh et al., 2008; Knapp et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2013), and the tail and spinal cord of salamander, fish, and Xenopus (this study and Caubit et al., 1997; Stoick-Cooper, 2007; Hui et al., 2014; Sugiura, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to studies in different regenerative systems.

claim: In zebrafish fin regeneration, constitutive overexpression of Wnt5 halts regeneration.
source: In zebrafish fin regeneration, constitutive overexpression of Wnt5 halts regeneration while in Xenopus, grafting Wnt5-expressing cells yields the generation of a complete ectopic tail (Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007; Sugiura et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007 and Sugiura et al., 2009.

claim: In Xenopus, grafting Wnt5-expressing cells yields the generation of a complete ectopic tail.
source: In zebrafish fin regeneration, constitutive overexpression of Wnt5 halts regeneration while in Xenopus, grafting Wnt5-expressing cells yields the generation of a complete ectopic tail (Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007; Sugiura et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Stoick-Cooper et al., 2007 and Sugiura et al., 2009.

claim: Wnt5 gradients may implement PCP to re-establish the axis of polarity needed to drive polarized, regenerative tissue outgrowth.
source: Our study suggests that Wnt5 gradients may implement PCP to re-establish the axis of polarity needed to drive polarized, regenerative tissue outgrowth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about Wnt5a/b and PCP during axolotl spinal cord regeneration.

claim: By examining regenerative behaviors at cellular rather than tissue scale, PCP mechanisms were found to set the orientation and self-renewal properties of regenerative neural stem cells in the axolotl.
source: Here, by examining regenerative behaviors at cellular rather than tissue scale, we have found that the acquisition of an embryonic PNT-like signature includes the implementation of PCP mechanisms that set the orientation and self-renewal properties of regenerative neural stem cells in the axolotl.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings of the study.
